Climate & Environment
• Powerful storms bookend the Americas: a category-4 Hurricane Polo nears Baja California Sur while a nor’easter floods the US Northeast, killing at least one and cutting power to tens of thousands.
• Scientists warn a strong El Niño and a slow-moving Kelvin wave could lift California coastal sea levels by up to a foot, heightening storm surge and flood risks this winter.
• Scrutiny of data center emissions grows as an Australian mega-project in Sydney is scrapped amid policy/regulatory shifts and US developers are accused of skirting pollution controls.
• Water stress hits infrastructure and food systems: a burst Thames Water main left thousands without supply around London, and most of England’s essential crops are grown in drought-risk areas.
• Conservation signals are mixed: analysis credits Brazil’s Lula with sharply reduced Amazon deforestation, Biscayne Bay gains key habitat status, and sightings hint at a bogong moth rebound.
Why it matters: Intensifying climate extremes, stressed infrastructure, and shifting regulation are converging on energy, water, and land use — with direct implications for safety, food security, and investment.

• Iran publicly rejected US talks despite claims from Washington, underscoring continued regional tension.
Why it matters: Amid great-power thaw signals, unresolved flashpoints and mixed messaging continue to shape global trade and security risk.

• Two mass shootings in South Africa killed 28 amid persistent gang-related violence; fighting flared between rival forces and federal troops in Somalia’s Baidoa.
• Ethiopia accused Sudan and Egypt of backing Tigray rebels; Sudan’s army denied it and pointed to internal Ethiopian dynamics.
• Reports that OpenAI agents repeatedly scanned a UN website highlight an emerging cyber risk vector from autonomous tools.
Why it matters: Conventional and hybrid threats — from local armed clashes to terrorism and AI-enabled cyber incidents — are testing security responses across regions.

Entertainment.title: Burton Raids Zeb Powell's Wardrobe for "Zeb's Closet," a Baggy Outerwear Collection
Entertainment.text: SummaryBurton's first globally available outerwear and apparel collection with Zeb Powell pairs waterproof shells and utility details with his signature oversized fitsThe lineup spans heavyweight hoodies, jerseys, rugby shirts, shorts, reversible bucket hats and a reversible insulated vest designed for layeringA traveling installation called Zeb's Mobile Closet debuts in New York City before visiting key snowboarding destinations around the worldBurton has launched Zeb's Closet, an outerwear and apparel collection built in partnership with team rider Zeb Powell. Burton bills it as the first globally available collection it has created with the snowboarder. The range is designed around Powell's personal style rather than performance specs alone, combining technical outerwear with the loose, oversized pieces he wears both on the mountain and off it.The design brief was simple: build what Powell would actually wear. In practice, that means waterproof outerwear, utility-driven detailing and premium construction, all cut into the roomy, baggy silhouettes closely tied to his look. Every piece is meant to allow unrestricted movement, so the fit supports the loose, freestyle way he rides.The rest of the range pushes further into streetwear. Heavyweight hoodies, jerseys, rugby shirts, tees, shorts and pants sit alongside reversible bucket hats and technical shells. All of it is intended to be stacked in layers and worn long after the last lap of the day. The standout piece is a reversible insulated vest, which gives riders a functional mid-layer with enough personality to wear on its own."It's called Zeb's Closet because it's actually what I would wear - on the mountain and off the mountain," Powell said in a statement. That on-and-off-hill crossover fits the larger picture Burton sees in the collection. The brand views Powell as the face of a new generation of snowboarding shaped by creativity, self-expression and the communities changing what the sport looks like. "Zeb has inspired an entirely new generation to see snowboarding differently," said Zach Nigro, Burton's Vice President of Brand & Sports Marketing.That community focus extends to the rollout through Zeb's Mobile Closet, a custom-built traveling installation modeled on Powell's own closet. The installation debuts in New York City during launch week before heading to snowboarding hubs around the world. At each stop, riders can see the collection, meet Powell and join local events, ride days and park sessions. The installation will change as the season goes on, appearing at flagship retail events and on-hill activations, and at some stops it will even be built into the terrain as a rideable feature.Zeb's Closet is available now online, Burton retail stores and select specialty retailers worldwide.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

The theme is time itself, including both its rewards and its toll, and how it shapes the brand's recurring cast of "Protagonists." In practice, that idea shows up in clothing designed to age well: everyday staples built to work across seasons, climates and settings.Fabric is central to the collection. The approach fits how the label works overall: every garment is designed, tested and made in New York City using performance-focused Japanese materials.Several returning staples now come in heavier fabrics. The brand's signature pant comes back in a heavyweight cotton-nylon with added water repellency, making it more suited to bad weather. The returning shirt and suiting move into weightier cotton-silk blends and textured poly wool twills, giving the tailoring more structure for colder months.The newer pieces build on earlier designs. The full-zip sweater updates a past model in a double-face fleece that is both heavier and softer to the touch. The technical jacket from Spring/Summer 2026 also returns in a more refined version, now made in mid-weight Ventile with a DWR finish, with hidden chest and hand pockets, and with pleating across the back that gives it a rounder shape.The most notable addition is the new High Pile Fleece Vest. Entertainment.title: Tan Suan: Reshaping Time Beneath Light and Shadow
Entertainment.text: For Hypebeast China's latest digital cover, we have no interest in retelling the overnight-success myth of a fashion influencer. Instead, through Tan Suan, we want to reflect how an entire generation of young women creators grows and defines itself as time moves forward. Her path from individual creator to a broader cultural presence also offers a window into how China's new generation of creative talent is being seen by the world, and how it is starting to shape global fashion and luxury culture.In an era that treats "effortlessness" as gospel, ease is the aesthetic face she presents to the world. Her deep reverence for the craft and her constant self-scrutiny are the homework she keeps for herself. The outside world tends to reduce top-tier access, flawless polish and an idealized life into data points and labels. On the other side of the light is her clear-headed reflection. Social media may capture her present, but it cannot simply define what kind of woman she is. Her humility and focus, her habit of "keeping herself low," is not timidity. It is a creator's deepest instinct: to avoid the floating froth of a restless visual tide and build her own aesthetic order and artistic perspective.This is not only about Tan Suan. It captures a moment in which women creators are moving from "being looked at" to "expressing themselves." They are no longer content to be pretty faces generating noise and numbers in front of the camera. Over time, they are turning the camera into an extension of self-expression and artistic exploration. In fast-cycling pop culture, she delivers liveliness and cool with precision in front of the lens. Behind it, she quietly refines the aesthetic logic behind her content, her deeper understanding of style, and the ultimate question of "who am I."Tan Suan's trajectory also offers an entry point into how Chinese creative culture is changing. In the past, young Chinese creators were largely watched and defined within the context of global fashion and pop culture. Today, more and more of China's new creative talent is entering conversations around global fashion and luxury on the strength of their own taste, visual language and cultural experience, and becoming part of what shapes trends and sets context. Tan Suan is a powerful case study for this narrative. As China's cultural influence keeps reaching outward, how do young creators carry their own perspective onto the world stage, and redefine what "from China" means in a global context?This cover, then, is an in-depth conversation with the social media filter stripped away. Using Tan Suan as our subject, we try to glimpse the inner world beneath the images and symbols, and to explore how a woman, shaped by time, grows a soul and a sense of self with real depth. Through her personal journey, we also revisit the cultural migration now underway among China's new generation of creators on the world stage. Refusing to be defined by social media and retreating to the low, deep places within has become her strongest armor. Because only by letting time settle can she keep both feet on the ground, and, amid ever-shifting trends, grow a genuine strength of her own that outlasts both traffic and the years.If you divided your life so far into stages, how would you split it? What moments mark the dividing lines?I feel my life so far really only has two stages. I haven't lived enough yet to break it down that finely. Before 25 was the first stage, when I didn't truly know myself. Now I've just stepped into the second stage, where I'm figuring myself out.You started facing the camera very early, and went from "being seen" to enormous exposure. Looking back, do you think being seen really equals being understood?For me, being seen is often more like the beginning of being misunderstood. The internet puts a filter over everyone through the screen. What people see are compressed fragments, not a three-dimensional, real you.From the outside, your liveliness on camera looks effortless. But behind the camera, what's the most serious work you've done to build an aesthetic logic that doesn't just follow the crowd?I'm actually someone who tries really hard. My personality is fairly low-key at its core, but the version of me online is much more lively. The most serious work is probably thinking every day about what content to make, how to edit it and how to write the script.Whether it's high luxury or streetwear, you always make it your own. How do you fuse pieces that seem to come from different worlds into a visual rule that's distinctly "Tan Suan"?There's no complicated rule. I just go by instinct and my own taste. A lot of the time it's simply that a combination feels more right on me, more like me. Apart from special occasions like shows, where I wear a brand's total look, in private I don't really like wearing head-to-toe luxury.When you're feeling drained and lost in real life, but the camera needs you to deliver your coolest, most perfect self, how do you handle the relationship between "Tan Suan" and "Zhuang Fei"?When I feel drained or lost, I choose to pause and give myself space to rest and reset. I don't like bringing negative energy online to everyone. Once I've sorted myself out, I start again.Today, when algorithms and traffic quantify everything, creators can easily become "models" stripped of their agency. When did you realize you were no longer just a subject being watched, but a creator in control?When I stopped thinking only about traffic when I posted, I could make the content I genuinely wanted to share. If everything you post is driven by traffic, you lose what makes you unique and become a symbol anyone could replace at any moment. Whether I'm shooting content or going to fashion week, as long as I'm fully immersed in something I find interesting, I don't think much about outside factors.As an online "curator," how do you decide what's worth being seen now? Is there anything you love but would never post?I think about how to blend my personal style naturally into everyday life. As for what I'd never post: I secretly love dancing, but I'll never put it online, hahaha, because my dancing is honestly a bit "scary."You've been invited to major fashion weeks many times and appeared in campaigns for major luxury houses. If you placed yourself today within the global fashion context, what do you think you actually bring?A personal style that belongs to an ordinary girl, I suppose. I'm not tall, and I'm not the flawless "template beauty" of conventional standards. But I think the world's idea of beauty should be diverse. There are countless girls like me out there, and they deserve to be seen too.In a content battlefield where things turn over by the second, how do you see time and age shaping a woman creator? Are you afraid of being replaced by a younger algorithm, or do you look forward to time giving you deeper experience?I think women at every age have a charm unique to that stage. Ten years ago, I never would have imagined I'd be going to fashion week shows. Rather than fearing being phased out by the algorithm, I'm more excited about the experiences and perspective time will bring me.You've said that when you modeled for Taobao in high school, you just wanted to "earn some pocket money." What has fundamentally changed about your ambition since then?Honestly, not much. As a kid, my dream was to be able to buy clothes I liked and travel to cities I wanted to see. It's pretty much the same now.Social platforms keep pushing creators to cater to their logic and make the content they favor. Have you ever felt pressured by that kind of "authority," or do you not care at all?More or less, yes. For example, when a platform launches a new trending topic or campaign, they want you to produce content following a set template. I'm not great at saying no, but within those frameworks, I insist on doing it my own way and in my own style.Beyond the spotlight and countless cameras, what does your most treasured private time look like? How do those unrecorded hours feed back into your work?Probably lying at home when I'm not working, ordering a pile of takeout and watching movies, or going to a friend's place to chat and play games, just zoning out. That offline time is extremely important to me. If I were always in that tense, on-camera state, I'd feel like I'd become a fake person living inside a digital network.Years from now, in this complicated era, which side of Tan Suan do you hope people remember?That she was a pretty good style creator. Entertainment.title: The World's First ‘Minecraft’ Roller Coaster Launches Riders Out of the Nether
Entertainment.text: SummaryEscape the Nether puts riders in minecarts alongside Steve and Alex, fighting through hostile mobs and plenty of lava before launching back to the OverworldThe Minecraft Hotel features Nether Portal-inspired lifts, mine-tunnel corridors and bedrooms styled with the game's blocks, items, mobs and texturesBoth attractions anchor Minecraft World, a new land opening at Chessington World of Adventures Resort in 2027Minecraft is getting its first roller coaster, Escape the Nether, as the headline ride of Minecraft World, a new land coming to Chessington World of Adventures Resort in southwest London in 2027. Alongside it is the Minecraft Hotel, the first official hotel built around the game. The land is being developed by Mojang Studios and Merlin Entertainments.Escape the Nether starts, like the game, in a minecart. Riders board and join Steve and Alex, Minecraft's default playable characters, on a run through the Nether, the game's fiery underworld dimension. Along the way they face hostile mobs head-on before a launch sends them back to the Overworld. The Nether setting also means the ride's scenery features lava throughout.The hotel is themed from the moment guests arrive. Check-in is designed to look like the Overworld, with blocky trees and animals setting the scene. The lifts are styled after Nether Portals, and the hallways are built to look like mine tunnels, so getting to a room feels like exploring the game.The bedrooms, which the hotel calls "respawn points," bring the game's visual style into real life. Rooms are designed with Minecraft's blocks, items, mobs, textures and colors, aiming to appeal to longtime players and newcomers alike.Food and drink follow the same approach, each tied to a specific part of the game. The restaurant is underwater-themed, inspired by Minecraft's ocean biomes. The bar is modeled on the Woodland Mansion, and its drinks are styled as the game's colorful potions. Beyond the ride and hotel, the wider land will include areas based on the Overworld's lush caves, mineshafts and plains, along with mob meet-and-greets, play areas and themed shops.Minecraft World, Escape the Nether and the Minecraft Hotel are set to open at Chessington World of Adventures Resort in 2027, with an exact date yet to be announced.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Science & Technology.title: Here’s How Delhi Achieved Its Epic Power-Grid Fix
Science & Technology.text: It’s 6 a.m. on a cold January morning in 2002 in New Delhi. It’s still dark outside, and I’m in the kitchen preparing breakfast, packing lunches, and getting my two children ready to catch the school bus when, for the third time in a week, the power goes out. No lights, no mixer to finish my daughter’s puttu—her favorite rice dish—no kettle, no toaster. The bathroom is dark, and the kids are upset.It will probably be hours before the power comes back on, so I grab a flashlight and light the candles that are set up around the house for these occasions. We’re behind schedule now. We pack the food we have, bundle up as the house turns chilly, and head outside, leaving a mess in the kitchen. We make our way to the bus stop in the dark—the streetlights are out, too—only to discover my daughter has missed her ride. Again. I’ll be late for work at Jamia Millia Islamia, a university where I am a professor of electrical engineering and teach power systems and smart grids. I just hope the power is on there.This was a common scene for my family and all of Delhi in the early 2000s. Power outages happened almost daily and lasted hours. When the power was on, the quality was so poor that it would dim lights, flicker screens, and wreak havoc on appliances. Customer service at the power utilities essentially didn’t exist. A child walks in July 2007 past a store in New Delhi specializing in reconditioned generators. The fear of power cuts during summer heat spurs demand for these generators so that residents can produce their own power.Nicholas Bradley/AFP/Getty ImagesThese problems had been getting worse through the 1980s and 1990s. The cause: an aging distribution grid bereft of crucial technologies, and electricity providers with little accountability. The situation became so bad that the city was losing more than half of its power through obsolete equipment and theft. These staggering losses meant that utilities got paid for only a fraction of the electricity they were trying to deliver. And the lack of funds prevented them from investing in better grid infrastructure.But over the last quarter century, a remarkable effort by the government and the city’s distribution utilities has turned Delhi’s grid into a reliable, modern system. Power losses have shrunk from over 50 percent in 2002 to 5 to 6 percent in 2026—on par with France and Belgium, and better than Greece and Serbia. Delhi’s grid reliability index, a measure of how often electricity can be counted on, stood at around 70 percent in 2002 and has now topped 99.9 percent. The bustling Main Bazar in the Paharganj neighborhood of Delhi increasingly uses more nighttime electricity, but reductions in electricity loss help counter demand.   iStock With reliable power, businesses across the city have blossomed. The streetlights are bright. The number of electric vehicles, including city buses, is growing daily. Quality of life has improved. Today, my family is comfortable year-round in our home despite Delhi’s scorching summers and cold winters. The chaos of losing power no longer hinders me from getting to work. The city still has problems—pollution, overcrowding, noise—but thankfully, reliable power is no longer among them.The transformation of Delhi’s grid can serve as a model for other cities that suffer from decrepit power infrastructure. Regions of Albania, Argentina, Bangladesh, Brazil, Estonia, India, Kenya, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Uganda, and Venezuela are reeling from heavy losses in their distribution grids. Their problems look like Delhi’s 25 years ago. I believe it’s possible to improve electricity in these places by adapting the changes Delhi made. Here’s an inside look at how the city accomplished it.Delhi’s Power Grid and Energy MixThe city of Delhi hosts the capital of the Republic of India, and sits along the Yamuna River in the northern part of the country. It’s home to about 23 million people and is one of the most densely populated areas in the world. Delhi’s grid includes thousands of kilometers of power lines, and peak electricity demand reached an all-time high this year of 8,748 megawatts. The city currently buys 76 percent of its power from central generating companies and private players from neighboring states. Energy generation within the city is restricted to natural gas and renewable sources. Nearly 48.5 percent of the city’s power comes from coal, about 26.5 percent from natural gas, and the rest from carbon-free sources, led by hydropower at 15.6 percent.  Tata Power replaced about 5 kilometers of overhead lines with underground cables, which reduced electricity loss and improved the aesthetics of Delhi’s streets, such as the Janta Flats in the Shalimar Bagh neighborhood.Tata Power-DDLBy the early 2000s, Delhi’s nearly 100-year-old power distribution system was in serious disrepair. Everything was old—lines, transformers, circuit breakers, switches. New grid technologies were needed to keep up with new kinds of electricity loads, but there was little money to upgrade components.The shabby state of the grid caused many problems, most notably high electricity losses, where electricity vanishes primarily as heat. The cause of the losses was a classic electrical problem: too much current flowing through a network that wasn’t designed to carry it efficiently.To understand the problem, it helps to understand how modern power grids work. Typically, they include generation, transmission, and distribution. After power is generated, transformers convert the electricity to high voltage levels—typically 132, 220, 400, or 765 kilovolts in India. Transmission lines then carry the power over long distances to receiving substations that are closer to where customers need electricity. Transformers then step down the voltage (to 66, 33, or 11 kV in India) and distribution lines branch out, carrying the power to customers. The whole grid works primarily on alternating current.Electricity Losses by Country, 2002 vs. 2023 Distribution networks carry both active and reactive power. Active power is the energy used to perform useful work (and is measured in watts). Reactive power is the power that flows back and forth in an electric circuit, building electric and magnetic fields (measured in volt-ampere-reactive, or VAR). Although it doesn’t perform useful work, reactive power is necessary for many devices, such as induction motors, transformers, and computers (typically any circuit or device with inductance or capacitance elements).When there are a lot of devices consuming reactive power on the same line, the overall current carried by the line—the sum of the active and reactive current—must increase. The more current in the line, the more the line heats up and the more energy that’s wasted as heat.In addition to current, resistance in the line will increase losses as well. Resistance is when electrons encounter opposition as they move through the conductive material (typically aluminum in a power grid). Longer lines with many branches and connection points will increase resistance. The rule of thumb is that line loss equals the square of the current multiplied by the resistance.Reactive power creates a second problem: It causes the voltage along the line to drop. And when the voltage falls, many modern electrical devices try to maintain roughly the same level of performance by drawing more current. That higher current produces even greater losses in the line and causes the voltage to fall further.Meter Technology Impacts Electricity LossesIn a healthy grid, the utility will take compensatory measures to lower the current and maintain the voltage all the way to the ends of the lines. But in Delhi, this wasn’t happening. The result was a vicious cycle. Reactive loads increased the current, the higher current increased energy losses and lowered the voltages, lower voltages forced devices to draw more current and further increased the losses.In some parts of Delhi, the effect was so severe that residents took matters into their own hands. A colleague of mine who lived in a different part of the city constantly experienced voltage that was too low for her appliances to operate reliably, so she had to install her own voltage stabilizer. At my home, we bought an inverter and battery system to keep a fan and a few lights running during the many outages.Electricity Loss and Theft in DelhiThe losses in Delhi weren’t caused solely by technical problems. Theft of electricity was rampant, by both the powerful and the powerless (in both senses of the word). Businesses, residential customers, and utility employees with vested interests would siphon electricity from the grid. It was easy to illegally hook into a streetlight or a distribution line running close to one’s house or factory. Utilities didn’t have the resources to identify theft or penalize offenders. Even if they could, the courts were already overburdened, and an electricity regulatory commission that could push for reforms had not yet fully formed.  Updated meters have made billing easier and more accurate.             Tata Power-DDL         Making matters worse, the utilities and their employees were rarely held accountable for their actions, and so corruption plagued the system. Junior engineers and line workers, many of them lacking appropriate technical skills, were tasked with handling nearly every issue, including outages, flickering, and bill payment. This was too much authority in the hands of people with too little training.On top of that, customers didn’t pay their bills. Meters were old, frequently faulty, and easily tampered with. Utility employees would take a meter reading by visiting the customer’s property, noting the reading in a book, entering it in a ledger or on a computer back at the office, and converting it into an electricity bill that would get dropped off at the customer’s property. This process left a lot of room for incorrect billing.To pay a bill, customers had to stand in long queues at the utility offices, which had limited business hours. Not wanting to take off a half day of work for this, many customers simply didn’t pay. And there was no penalty for not paying—there were no regulations allowing the utilities to cut off a customer’s power. (I paid my bill by having a family member stand in line for me.)The combined commercial and technical losses left Delhi’s utilities collecting payment for less than half of the electricity they were supplying in the early 2000s.India’s Electricity Act and Power ReformsSuch problems weren’t unique to Delhi. On average in 2002, state utilities across India experienced electricity losses of nearly 37 percent. My country desperately needed systemic reforms, but authority over electricity was split between the central and state governments so any decision-making was fractured. States managed most of the generation, as well as transmission and distribution, while the central government oversaw generation that supplied multiple states, such as hydropower, fossil fuel plants, and nuclear plants. The central government could push reforms, but the states determined whether those reforms would succeed. Making matters worse, most states put a single organization in charge of generation, transmission, and distribution, giving that entity too much control and reducing transparency and competition. A team of technicians with BSES Rajdhani Power maintains an insulator string on a large power transformer in 2011.  BSES Rajdhani Power In 2001, India’s central government began writing some historic legislation that became the landmark Electricity Act, 2003. Among the grand reforms aimed at transforming the country’s power industry, it unbundled state oversight of grid networks, creating separate entities for generation, transmission, and distribution. It also opened up the power sector to privatization. It allowed large electricity customers to bypass local distribution companies and purchase electricity from competitors or build their own power plants. It created a central regulatory agency responsible for determining interstate tariffs and promoting market competition in the power sector. And it created mechanisms for prosecuting electricity theft. Hundreds of capacitor banks have been installed in Delhi to supply reactive power at strategic locations and help stabilize voltage.Tata Power-DDLIn 2002, Delhi was already taking drastic action to fix its grid. The organization overseeing Delhi’s distribution, the Delhi Vidyut Board, was broken up and two private companies—BSES (now Reliance Infrastructure), and Tata Power—took over distribution. They faced a Herculean task. Tata Power, serving the northern half of Delhi, would have to tackle a combined commercial and technical electricity loss of 53.5 percent. BSES, whose territory was split between two subsidiaries, was facing 51.5 percent losses in South Delhi and 63.1 percent losses in East Delhi.“The company inherited a deteriorated and overloaded network, massive power theft, weak billing and collection systems, inaccurate consumer records, and an aging, largely untrained workforce,” Dwijadas Basak, CEO of Tata Power, told me. There were over 100,000 unresolved billing complaints, 20,000 pending connection applications, and frequent supply failures, which had severely eroded consumer trust, he added. Both Tata and BSES devised sweeping reforms and human resource development initiatives. The companies followed their own paths over the years, but ultimately implemented similar changes, with similar results.Delhi’s Electricity System OverhaulFixing Delhi’s grid was a journey that involved all stakeholders, including customers, city authorities, and utility employees at all levels. The utilities revamped their organizational structures, diminishing the power of junior staff and creating separate teams to focus on specific tasks. Long-term employees of the erstwhile Delhi Vidyut Board received training from the up-and-comers at the new companies.On the technical side, both companies installed digital control systems that let them monitor and operate the grid from a central location. Known as SCADA, or supervisory control and data acquisition, the systems offered a bird’s-eye view of the infrastructure, including the status of equipment, voltage, current, power flow, and switch positions, with updates in seconds. This helped the companies identify areas of high loss and theft and make faster decisions based on accurate information. The SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition) system at Balaji Estate in Delhi’s Kalkaji neighborhood serves as the nerve center of BSES Rajdhani Power’s distribution network in South and West Delhi. It enables real-time visibility, remote control of grid operations, fault identification and isolation, and load management. BSES Rajdhani PowerThe utilities also replaced aging transformers and circuit breakers and created extensive maintenance plans for equipment. In 2002, 11 percent of the transformers in the region were failing at any given time. That rate is less than 1 percent today, according to Tata. Crucially, the companies installed hundreds of capacitor banks, including some mobile ones, to supply reactive power at strategic locations. This improvement reduced the total current flowing in the distribution lines and helped stabilize the voltage. They also installed voltage regulators at points in the system where voltage tends to drop.To reduce theft, the companies replaced bare distribution wires with insulated lines—a single cable for three phases—which made it harder to tap into the lines. The cables also reduced outages because they’re better at preventing ground faults, which can occur when, say, a tree branch falls on the line.Workers received better sensors and tools to do their jobs safely and accurately. For instance, they were given helmet-mounted voltage sensors, which are safer than handheld ones, and thermal scanning tools to detect hidden defects in the insulation of high-voltage equipment that could otherwise have led to catastrophic failures.To reduce inaccurate billing and meter tampering, the companies replaced the old electromechanical meters with digital ones that are read with handheld devices. In some locations, radio-frequency-based group metering systems were installed by Tata to consolidate multiple customers’ meters into one. The data is then wirelessly transmitted to a central database, eliminating the need for individual meter readings. The companies are now trying smart meters, which give consumers more control over their electricity bills and give utilities remote control of some equipment (with the customer’s consent).To encourage people to pay their bills, the utilities installed kiosks that are available 24 hours a day, and they created a web-based payment system and mobile app. Incentives for early bill payment and community-engagement programs also helped. Assistance from Delhi’s law enforcement considerably reduced electricity theft. Tata Power hired women living in the 223 slums it serves in the northern parts of the city to knock on neighbors’ doors and remind them to pay their power bills. These payment collectors [left and center], known as abhas, were photographed while speaking with a customer [right] in the Sanjay Basti area of New Delhi in 2017. Prashanth Vishwanathan/Bloomberg/Getty Images In areas where theft was particularly rampant and losses were as high as 83 percent, according to Tata, the companies took a different strategy. These pockets of Delhi were predominantly occupied by low-income families. Tata Power, and later BSES, worked to improve the water supply for these residents and provide educational opportunities, such as instruction in reading and writing in Hindi as well as financial literacy. These efforts focused on the women, who were at home more, and paid them to collect electricity payments from their neighbors. Bill payment rates from these areas are now on par with those of other parts of Delhi.In recent years, some customers have been installing rooftop solar panels to take advantage of subsidies and incentives. This trend can reduce electricity losses further because the energy generated at the customer end reduces current in the distribution lines. Customers are also installing more LED lights and energy-efficient appliances, reducing the load in the system.BSES is using AI to help detect theft. The algorithms analyze consumption patterns in pockets where losses are higher than they should be. The company is also using AI to forecast demand, fine-tune operational efficiency, and provide chatbots for customers.Quality of Life Improves in DelhiLife in Delhi is better than it was 25 years ago. I’m not worried that the power may go out and force me to reschedule my activities. My uninterrupted Wi-Fi gives me peace of mind, and my heating and cooling systems keep me and my family comfortable. I rarely need to use our old inverter and battery. The sharp rise of e-rickshaws in Delhi has increased demand on the power grid.  Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images The number of businesses in Delhi has increased substantially, in part because of the access to quality power. People can confidently buy products that depend on electricity. In fact, the city’s peak electricity demand has tripled since 2002 due to the increase in population, commercial activity, and use of electrical gadgets.And then there’s the benefits to the planet. One unit of electricity that isn’t frittered away is one less unit that must be generated, not to mention the reductions in carbon emissions.Still, there’s work to do. Some areas of Delhi continue to have high losses, driven partly by the illegal charging of e-rickshaws. Elsewhere in India, the states of Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Telangana still experience losses of about 17 to 23 percent despite the sweeping Electricity Act, 2003. There are many reasons for the ongoing losses: long distribution lines to remote villages, less digitization, and inefficiencies in billing and collection of payments.These regions, and others around the world, can learn from Delhi’s grid comeback. Recently, power losses have increased substantially in countries such as Argentina, Greece, Jamaica, and Morocco, according to the World Bank, and some of the causes are similar to those that Delhi faced back in 2002.Meanwhile, Australia, most countries in North America and Europe, and a few countries in Asia and Africa experience low electricity losses as they invest regularly in their distribution infrastructure and the ethical enforcement of rules. In China, for example, losses have gradually been cut in half, from 7.1 to 3.4 percent. In Latvia, losses plummeted from 25 to 5.8 percent.What’s important is a comprehensive approach. Technologies like smart metering, AI, and analytics certainly help, but equally important is that people in the field are trained and take responsibility for their jobs, and that laws are enforced and payments collected.“Sustainable loss reduction cannot happen through technology alone,” Abhishek Ranjan, CEO of BSES Rajdhani Power told me. “Technology is an important enabler, but long-term success comes from combining it with disciplined execution, operational accountability, and strong consumer engagement.”

Science & Technology.title: AFTERSHOCK's $14,200 USD Cherry Bloom Gaming PC Has 70 Hand-Painted Titanium Petals That Bloom With Heat
Science & Technology.text: SummaryAFTERSHOCK released the Cherry Bloom, a $14,200 gaming rig built around a kinetic cherry blossom sculptureThe interior features 70 hand-formed titanium petals that physically curl open as the system heats upThe hardware is powered by a Ryzen 7 9800X3D processor, a Zotac RTX 5080 GPU and 64GB of memoryAFTERSHOCK has officially launched the Cherry Bloom. This $14,200 USD rig features a heat-reactive cherry blossom tree planted inside the chassis and is billed as the world's first blooming gaming PC. The entire build sits securely inside an APNX V2 chassis wrapped in glass across a full 270 degrees.Seventy hand-formed and hand-painted blossoms make up the system's kinetic center. A titanium alloy specifically engineered to react to heat comprises these blossoms. The mechanical movement relies entirely on the metal responding to temperature without using motors, software firmware or RGB lighting. A demonstration shows the Cherry Bloom sitting fully closed at a resting temperature of 18 degrees Celsius. As internal temperatures rise, the metal petals physically curl open before folding shut once the machine cools.A Ryzen 7 9800X3D processor paired with a Zotac RTX 5080 graphics card powers the rig. The system pushes output using 64 gigabytes of DDR5-6000 memory and a 2TB PCIe Gen4 SSD. This build includes a 1300W Platinum power supply to support the components. While the titanium tree provides the visible mechanical display, a custom open-loop liquid cooling system handles the internal thermal load.The Cherry Bloom hit the market priced at roughly $14,200 USD, converted from an asking price of $19,995 AUD. Customers can order the machine now with next-business-day dispatch, though the price does not include shipping. This strategy reflects a luxury approach where the engineering and hand-finishing of reactive metal petals account for much of the cost. By turning exhaust heat into a visible display, the system transforms thermal management into kinetic art.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast
